opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For us at InferAct, the starting point is simple: we think the open-source inference ecosystem is becoming core infrastructure, much like Linux became for operating systems. So our priorities this year really come down to three things.

The first is keeping vLLM healthy as a truly open, community-driven project. A lot of what we do day to day isn't flashy. It's reviewing pull requests, keeping the CI stable, and making sure that when a new model comes out, whether from a Chinese lab or an American lab, people can run it on day zero. That breadth is a big part of the value. If we only optimized for one company's hardware or one company's models, we would lose what makes the project useful.

The second is the hardware side. The accelerator landscape is getting much more diverse: NVIDIA, AMD, TPUs, and a lot of domestic chips here in China. Every vendor wants to plug into the ecosystem. So we've spent a lot of effort on clean abstractions, things like the plugin system and a cleaner separation between the model code and the hardware backends. That way a chip vendor can maintain their own backend without forking the whole project. Forks are really painful for everyone, so reducing fragmentation is a priority.

The third is the shift in workloads. Two years ago inference mostly meant chatbots: one request in, one response out. Now it's agents, very long contexts, reinforcement learning rollouts, and large MoE models served across many nodes. That changes the problem. You have to think about prefill-decode disaggregation, KV cache that lives beyond a single GPU, expert parallelism, and scheduling across a cluster instead of on one machine. A lot of our engineering this year goes into making those distributed setups something an ordinary team can deploy, not just the top few labs.

I'd also add a philosophical point. People sometimes ask why we start a company instead of keeping it purely academic. My answer is that the project has reached a scale where it needs full-time people who are accountable for it, and the commercial side should support the open-source side, not the reverse. Our guiding question is always whether something makes open-source inference better for everyone. If the answer is yes, we do it.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing workloads such as agents, long contexts, and MoE serving, but does not identify how people use tokens as a workload consideration.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about priorities, I try to start from what the ecosystem actually looks like right now, because the inference layer has changed a lot in the past year or two.

A few years ago, the hard problem was just making serving work at all: getting a model to run on a GPU with reasonable throughput, handling batching, not running out of memory. Those problems are largely solved in the sense that there are good open-source answers to them. What's changed is that models themselves have become much more heterogeneous. You have mixture-of-experts models with very different memory and communication patterns than dense models. You have long-context models where the KV cache is the real bottleneck. You have multimodal models that mix a vision encoder, a language decoder, sometimes an audio component, each with its own compute profile. And on the hardware side, you no longer have one dominant target. There are many accelerators, many interconnect topologies, and a lot of people running on whatever they can get.

So the first priority, in my view, is keeping the framework truly general without letting it become a pile of special cases. It's very tempting, when a new model architecture comes out, to add a dedicated code path for it. Do that twenty times and you have something nobody can maintain. The discipline we try to hold is to ask what abstraction this new model is really exposing that we didn't have before, and to add that abstraction rather than the special case. That's slow in the short term and much faster in the long term.

The second priority is the hardware story. If open-source inference only works well on one vendor's chips, then it isn't really open in a meaningful sense. The ecosystem is healthier when the same model definition can run across different backends and users can make hardware decisions based on cost and availability rather than being locked in by the software. That requires clean separation between the model layer, the scheduler, and the kernel layer, and a lot of unglamorous work on plugin interfaces and testing infrastructure so that contributors from different hardware vendors can land their work without stepping on each other.

Third, and I think this is underrated, is reliability and predictability in production. A lot of the benchmarks people publish are peak-throughput numbers under ideal conditions. Real deployments care about tail latency, about what happens when requests have wildly different lengths, about not crashing at three in the morning. Open-source systems historically had a reputation for being fast but rough. Closing that gap, making the default configuration something you can actually run a business on, is a priority that doesn't show up on leaderboards but matters enormously for adoption.

And then there's the community aspect itself. The reason open-source inference has progressed this fast is that the people who build models, the people who make chips, and the people who run services all contribute to the same codebase. Each group sees problems the others can't. Keeping that collaboration healthy, having clear review processes, good documentation, a roadmap people can actually see and influence, is as much a technical priority as any kernel optimization, because it determines whether the project is still moving quickly two years from now.

If I had to compress all of that into one sentence: this year is less about proving that open-source inference can be fast, and more about proving that it can be the stable, general foundation that the rest of the stack builds on.

r001.rationale: The response treats token-related workload variation as an inference priority: it notes long contexts make KV cache a bottleneck and that production requests have wildly different lengths.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the priorities around making inference faster, easier to operate, and easier to contribute to. I don’t want to present that as a formal roadmap, but that’s how I think about what matters for the ecosystem.

Performance is a big part of it, of course. But a throughput improvement only helps if it carries over to the workloads people actually run, with their latency requirements and resource constraints. So we need to look at efficiency together with reliability and usability.

For open source, the other priority is making the work cumulative. Can someone add support for a model or a piece of hardware without creating a separate stack they have to maintain forever? Can they reproduce a performance result and understand why it improved? Making that contribution process easier is how you turn individual optimizations into progress for the whole ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response mentions real workloads, latency requirements, and resource constraints, but does not identify how people use tokens as a workload consideration.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame the priorities around making inference more efficient, more reliable, and easier to use. Performance matters, but we should measure it under realistic workloads: what latency users experience, how much throughput you can sustain, and what it costs to serve the model.

For the open-source ecosystem, supporting new models and hardware is also important. People should be able to adopt improvements without rebuilding their entire serving stack. That takes good interfaces, testing, documentation, and collaboration with the community.

So my view is that we should focus on improvements that translate into practical benefits for developers. A benchmark result is useful, but the real test is whether people can deploy it and see the benefit in their own applications.

r001.rationale: The response mentions realistic workloads, latency, throughput, and serving cost, but does not identify how people use tokens as a workload consideration.
